title: Lesson 28: High-Volume Event Patterns: Streaming, Pacing, and Platform Event Limits
description: What changes when event volume stops being a trickle and becomes a flood: streaming with the Pub/Sub API, pacing publish rates against rolling limits, and the platform event allocations that decide whether your bus survives the day.

questions.question: A streaming subscriber disconnects for a few hours. Why can it catch up later without losing the events it missed?
options: The bus retains messages for a fixed window, so the subscriber resumes from its last position.
The producer keeps republishing every single message until each subscriber acknowledges that it received it.
The subscriber polls the bus for any missed events once it has reconnected successfully.
Delivery is guaranteed only to subscribers that stay connected the whole time.
questions.explanation: Messages persist in the bus for a bounded retention window, so a subscriber that saved its position replays from there and closes the gap left by the disconnect.

questions.question: A consumer relies on the order in which events published through separate publish calls arrive. What is true about that order?
options: Order is guaranteed across calls because the platform routes each org through one server.
Order is guaranteed within a single publish call but not across separate calls.
Order is never guaranteed, even within a single publish call.
Order is guaranteed only for change-data events, not for platform events.
questions.explanation: Events in one publish call keep their passed order, but separate requests can be handled by different servers at different speeds, so cross-call order is not something to depend on.

questions.question: An org with a fixed daily delivery allocation streams the same events to two external subscribers. How is its usage counted?
options: Once per message, since delivery counts the event and not the subscriber.
Only for subscribers that sit outside the org, and only for platform events.
Per subscriber, so two subscribers draw the same shared pool twice over.
Not at all, because the delivery allocation does not apply to streaming subscribers.
questions.explanation: Delivery usage is counted for each subscribed client and added across subscribers, so adding a consumer is a second charge against the same pool rather than a free read.
